native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 cohort, increased time preference — proxied by more impatient savings behavior in 1989 (taking money out of savings rather than putting money in) — is associated with slightly higher BMI, but the association is small and cross-sectional, not causal. One step toward more impatient savings behavior (put-in → no-change → took-out) is associated with +0.16 BMI units (95% CI 0.002–0.322, p=0.047) adjusting for age, sex, race, 1989 income and 1985 wealth (n=5,665); raw group means: put-in 24.69 vs no-change 25.26 vs took-out 25.25 vs no-savings 25.45 (4-group ANOVA F=7.25, p<0.001). Read as a weak positive association between impatience and weight, not evidence that impatience leads to higher BMI.
native_result.WorkflowB: NLSY79 raw (12,686x61, 0 dup IDs). Weight 1989/1992 interpreted as POUNDS despite metadata saying kg (median 158, sex split M=175/F=135, implied BMI mean 25.2 vs 55.5 if kg); height 1985 in inches (M=70/F=64.2); height 1981 in inconsistent units (implied BMI 36.9) excluded. BMI = weight_1989(lb->kg)/(height_1985(in->m))^2, same interview year as savings behavior. Time-preference proxy = 1989 savings-flow direction: put-in=-1, no-change=0, took-out=+1; no-savings excluded from primary, kept in 4-group robustness. Listwise deletion (n 10,167 -> 5,665 with covariates); income/wealth log+winzor p99.5 for top-codes; weight winzor p99.5 sensitivity. Primary OLS (HC1) + group t-test/ANOVA; robustness: 4-group ANOVA (incl. no-savings), BMI 1992, winzorized weight, continuous net savings flow (log1p SIN - log1p SOUT), Pearson/Spearman correlations.

sub_hypo.text: In the NLSY79 cohort, more impatient savings behavior in 1989 is weakly associated with higher BMI, adjusting for age, sex, race, 1989 income, and 1985 wealth; this cross-sectional association is not causal.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents with complete primary-analysis data and covariates (n=5,665 after listwise deletion), excluding respondents reporting no savings in 1989.
variables: Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989
Age of respondent at interview date, 1989
Total net family income, previous calendar year, 1989
sub_hypo.relations: Savings behavior is coded put-in=-1, no-change=0, took-out=+1, with increasing values representing greater impatience. Each one-step increase is associated with +0.16 BMI units (95% CI 0.002–0.322; p=0.047) in adjusted OLS with HC1 standard errors. BMI is calculated from 1989 weight interpreted as pounds and converted to kilograms, divided by squared 1985 height converted from inches to meters. Income and wealth are log-transformed and winsorized at the 99.5th percentile. The association is small, positive, cross-sectional, and noncausal.

sub_hypo.text: Unadjusted BMI differs across the four 1989 savings-behavior groups in the NLSY79 cohort, with lower mean BMI among respondents putting money into savings than among the other groups.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 cross-sectional four-group comparison of 1989 savings behavior and BMI, including respondents reporting no savings.
variables: Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989
sub_hypo.relations: Mean BMI is 24.69 for put-in, 25.26 for no-change, 25.25 for took-out, and 25.45 for no-savings; four-group ANOVA F=7.25, p<0.001. BMI uses 1989 weight interpreted as pounds and 1985 height in inches, converted to kilograms and meters. These unadjusted group differences do not establish causation.
